result: {"summary":"Independent MR-3 readiness review of the attached-manager ticket retry/release path (src/store/attached/invocation.rs, src/store/attached/driver.rs, src/runner/linux/runtime.rs, src/machine/manager/release.rs, src/store/machine_ticket.rs), scoped to transient waiting retries, outbox compaction, transmission-clock freshness, cancellation and lost replies. The core retry design is sound and I could confirm its central invariant from code: the local outcome table is written only by a trigger that fires on *rejected* outcomes, so a ticketed operation can never satisfy retry_waiting_attached_ticket's join, and the operation_id swap makes an old waiting reply unable to authorize a newly enqueued command; compaction of attached_outbox after the trigger fires is genuinely safe, and release.rs's post-commit re-check producing NeverReleased (rather than replaying consumption) is correct. I did not confirm final acceptance readiness. Two high-severity safety/liveness issues stand out: (1) Driver::connect empties the barrier registry with mem::take, so an already-transmitted AuthorizeInvocation re-transmitted after a reconnect is given a brand-new freshness clock — if the coordinator idempotently replays the earlier Ticket, fresh() no longer bounds mint-to-release latency, and nothing in release_with_clock inspects ticket.issued_unix_millis or host_sample_unix_millis; (2) cancel and the local \"Ticket response deadline\" both abandon an operation that may still be transmitted and still mint a Ticket, leaving an unconsumed attached_tickets row with NULL cleanup_json that wedges the grant's cleanup chain. Several files that decide these outcomes (manager::pending, accept, super::queue::maintain, record_attached_cleanup, host_observation blocker codes, SessionIdentity.connection_epoch semantics) were not supplied; where the verdict depends on them I say so explicitly rather than asserting a bug.","findings":["HIGH (safety, mechanism code-confirmed / exploitability uncertain) — Reconnect re-mints the transmission clock for an operation that was already transmitted, defeating fresh(). Evidence: driver.rs Driver::connect() begins with `releases.disconnect()?`, and ReleaseState::disconnect() does `std::mem::take(&mut *self.barriers.lock()...)` — it REMOVES entries, then cancels the removed Arcs. Driver::step() then challenges every pending AuthorizeInvocation read from the durable outbox (`manager::pending`), with no filter on whether that operation was already sent; ReleaseState::challenge() finds a Vacant entry and constructs a fresh ReleaseBarrier, whose Challenge.clock is stamped at that moment (release.rs challenge_at). release.rs::challenge_at only suppresses re-stamping WITHIN one barrier object (`if let Some(old) = &state.challenge { ... return Ok(()) }`), so the documented invariant \"Retry keeps the ORIGINAL clock; reconnect needs a new Invocation challenge, never a rejuvenated ticket\" holds only for in-process retries, not across a transport reconnect. Failure trace: op1 challenged at T0 and transmitted; coordinator mints the Ticket (machine_ticket.rs authorize pushes intent into grant.tickets and returns InvocationTicket with issued_unix_millis/host_sample_unix_millis at T0) and the reply is lost; transport drops; Driver::drop -> disconnect() clears the map; new Driver::connect(); step() re-reads op1 as pending, challenge() creates a NEW barrier clocked at T0+N seconds; coordinator replays the same Ticket idempotently (MR-3 notes record idempotent replay as tested/passing); runtime.rs picks the ticket up and calls barrier.release(); release_with_clock compares only challenge.clock vs now — `fresh(challenge.clock, clock()?)` passes — and never compares ticket.issued_unix_millis or ticket.host_sample_unix_millis against the current clock, so an arbitrarily old Ticket, minted against an arbitrarily old coordinator-side resource/quiet admission, is committed and released. Residual defenses I could not verify: release_with_clock does check `state.session != ticket.session`, which would fence this IF manager::pending re-stamps the request with a session that differs per connection. That is doubtful from what is visible: driver.rs writes attached_peer only when absent (`if prior.is_none() { manager::bind(...) }`), so the peer session persists across reconnects, and the handshake validation compares machine_id/domain_id/manager_store_uuid/executor_incarnation but never connection_epoch. Please supply manager::pending and SessionIdentity.connection_epoch semantics. Remedy: persist a first-transmission clock per operation (e.g. attached_outbox.sent_unix/sent_monotonic written in the same tx as the send) and have ReleaseState::challenge refuse to mint a new clock for an operation already marked transmitted — such an operation must be rejected/cancelled and re-issued as a new intent rather than re-clocked; independently, add a mint-age check inside release_with_clock over ticket.issued_unix_millis and ticket.host_sample_unix_millis so freshness is anchored to the coordinator's decision, not to a local re-send; and bump connection_epoch on every connection so ticket.session cannot match a later connection's barrier.","HIGH (liveness + allocation wedging, code-confirmed up to three unsupplied functions) — Cancellation and the local ticket deadline abandon an in-flight AuthorizeInvocation without fencing it, so a Ticket can arrive for an invocation that has already been cleaned up, and its NULL cleanup permanently blocks the allocation's ticket chain. Evidence: runtime.rs execute() ticket loop returns Err on `lifecycle::pending_stop_verdict(...)` (cancel/timeout verdict) and on `Instant::now() >= until` (\"Invocation Ticket response deadline\"); neither path revokes the outbox operation enqueued by request_attached_ticket (invocation.rs `manager::enqueue(&tx, operation, &Command::AuthorizeInvocation{...})`). The cleanup closure then runs live.linux.cleanup(), record_attached_cleanup(job.invocation_id, ..., never=None) and live.linux_releases.retire(invocation) — retire() only removes/cancels the in-memory barrier. Failure trace: (1) driver is slow/reconnecting/paging recovery, so op1 is unanswered when `until` (default 5s for a non-quiet job: `job.spec.quiet.as_ref().map_or(5, |q| q.wait_budget_seconds.saturating_add(5))`) expires; (2) invocation fails and is cleaned up; (3) driver later transmits op1; machine_ticket.rs authorize() validates, executes `grant.tickets.push(intent.clone())` and `save_grant`, returning Outcome::Ticket; (4) accept() stores a row in attached_tickets with consumed=0 and cleanup_json NULL for a dead invocation; (5) the NEXT invocation on that allocation runs request_attached_ticket, which resolves `grant.tickets.last()` and reads `SELECT cleanup_json FROM attached_tickets WHERE invocation_id=?1`, gets NULL and returns StoreError::InvalidState(\"previous Invocation has no committed cleanup\"); coordinator-side validate_next() likewise rejects any successor with code \"cleanup_incomplete\", and per release.rs's own test seal_release() fails while a ticket lacks cleanup. Net effect: one racing cancel/timeout permanently wedges the Lease/Grant for both progress and sealing. Note the deadline path is not exotic — it is by construction the case where an operation is outstanding. Uncertainty I cannot resolve without the code: whether super::queue::maintain(&tx) (driver.rs step) cancels operations for abandoned invocations, whether accept() refuses a Ticket for an invocation with recorded cleanup, and whether record_attached_cleanup back-fills a later-arriving ticket row. Remedy: in the same transaction that records cleanup for an abandoned invocation, delete or tombstone that invocation's pending outbox operation and mark attached_local_invocations abandoned; make accept() route a Ticket for an abandoned invocation straight into record_cleanup/record_unused_cleanup using the already-durable proof, so the grant chain always advances.","MEDIUM-HIGH (liveness, code-confirmed) — The 250 ms freshness window must cover an entire cross-machine round trip plus a durable commit plus polling latency, and every overrun is a hard invocation failure. Evidence: release.rs fresh() requires `boot <= 250 && wall <= 250 && boot.abs_diff(wall) <= 50`; the clock is stamped in ReleaseState::challenge, which driver.rs step() calls immediately BEFORE `self.bridge.exchange(BridgeCommand::Exchange{...}, Instant::now() + Duration::from_secs(2))`. So the budget spans: bridge RTT to the Windows coordinator (allowed up to 2s by its own timeout), coordinator-side authorize() work, `tx.commit()` on the attached store (fsync), the runtime's `std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(5))` poll granularity, `lock(store)` acquisition contended against the runtime's own 5 ms polling of pending_stop_verdict/attached_ticket, live.linux.with_journal(journal.release_intent(&ticket)) and, for observed jobs, observation.with_release_sample(). Any exchange exceeding 250 ms guarantees `release_with_clock` returns Err(\"ticket is stale, canceled, used or locally unready\") after the coordinator has already pushed the intent into grant.tickets — burning one of the 256 slots enforced by validate_next's `grant.tickets.len() >= 256 => limit_exceeded` and requiring a whole new Invocation to retry. std::sync::Mutex is unfair, so N concurrent runners polling the Store every 5 ms can starve the driver thread and make overruns systemic rather than random. Remedy: compute the remaining budget before transmitting and skip/abort the exchange when the deadline cannot be met (fail before minting rather than after); surface a distinct retryable disposition for a stale-but-unconsumed ticket so the runner re-issues a new Invocation deterministically instead of failing the Attempt; and replace the runtime's 5 ms Store-lock poll with the existing ReleaseState wake/wait condvar to cut lock contention.","MEDIUM-HIGH (liveness/correctness, code-confirmed) — Transmission of AuthorizeInvocation is not gated on connected=1/reconciliation, so a reconnect during a ticket wait deterministically produces a Ticket the executor is forbidden to consume. Evidence: driver.rs connect() sets `UPDATE attached_local_mode SET connected=0` and only Outcome::Reconciled restores `connected=1`; step() transmits whatever manager::pending returns with no connected check; but invocation.rs consume() rejects with \"Ticket belongs to a disconnected or different Invocation generation\" whenever `connected != Some(true)`. Failure trace: invocation is waiting on op1; transport blips; new Driver::connect() sets connected=0 and begins recovery; step() finds op1 pending (recovery paging is only enqueued in the `manager::pending(...).is_none()` branch, so op1 is transmitted first, ahead of reconciliation); coordinator mints a Ticket; runtime.rs breaks its loop, retry_waiting_attached_ticket stops firing (its `NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM attached_tickets ...)` guard), barrier.release() runs commit -> mark_started_with_ticket/authorize_*_with_ticket -> consume() -> InvalidState because connected is still 0. The invocation fails, the ticket is left unconsumed, and case 2 above applies to its cleanup. Remedy: hold AuthorizeInvocation in the outbox until connected=1 (or explicitly prefer recovery/reconciliation commands over authorization commands in the pending selection), so the coordinator is never asked to mint a Ticket the executor cannot legally consume.","MEDIUM (correctness, hazard confirmed / classification unverifiable from supplied files) — Retryability of a rejection is decided by a hardcoded string list that is decoupled from the code that produces those strings, so a transient resource-contention rejection can be misclassified as fatal. Evidence: invocation.rs waiting_outcome() matches exactly `\"quiet_waiting\" | \"quiet_contaminated\" | \"detector_unavailable\" | \"observation_stale\" | \"observation_missing\" | \"observation_unusable\" | \"observed_resource_busy\" | \"unavailable\"`. machine_ticket.rs authorize() emits `Outcome::Rejected { code: blocker.code, detail: blocker.detail }` where `waiting = resource_blockers.first().or(context.non_quiet_blockers.first())` and `resource_blockers = physical.blockers(&readiness.config.resources, &active, &readiness.config.impact_incompatibilities)`. Only two producer codes are verifiable from the supplied text: \"quiet_waiting\" (in the list, correct) and \"quiet_unattainable\" (deliberately excluded and asserted terminal by the unit test). The codes minted by physical.blockers() for cpu_units/ram_mb/cargo_slots/gpu_slots/impacts, and by evaluate_request's non_quiet_blockers, are in files not supplied. If any of them is, say, \"resource_busy\" or \"cargo_slots_exhausted\" rather than \"observed_resource_busy\", then runtime.rs's `lock(store)?.attached_ticket(...)` turns a \"wait for a free slot\" answer into `StoreError::InvalidState(\"Invocation Ticket request did not grant release: ...\")` and the invocation fails immediately instead of waiting out its budget — precisely the managed-Cargo contention path MR-3 exercises. Remedy: stop classifying on strings — carry retryability in the type (`Outcome::Rejected { code, detail, retryable: bool }` or a shared `enum BlockerCode`) so the coordinator that mints the blocker declares its transience; failing that, add a test that enumerates every Blocker code constructible by physical.blockers()/evaluate_request and asserts its waiting_outcome classification.","MEDIUM (correctness/liveness, code-confirmed in the supplied file) — A probe can never be re-authorized on its own Grant after a never-released or stale ticket. Evidence: machine_ticket.rs validate_next(): `AllocationOwner::Probe { invocation_id, .. } => previous.is_none() && intent.role == InvocationRole::Probe && ...`. For Work owners the file explicitly supports retry-in-place — `(InvocationRole::Primary, InvocationRole::Primary, false) => intent.role_index == 0` and `(Postcondition, Postcondition, false) => intent.role_index == last.role_index` — but the Probe arm has no analogue, so once one intent is in grant.tickets, any successor intent is rejected with code \"conflict\". Failure trace: probe invocation gets a Ticket; the release misses the 250 ms window (see the freshness finding) or yields Disposition::NeverReleased; cleanup is recorded with user_code_released=false; a retry on the same probe Lease/Grant is structurally impossible, so a single transient delay consumes the probe's whole allocation. This is safe (nothing is released twice) but converts a transient fault into an allocation-level failure. Confirm the runner obtains a fresh probe Lease/Grant in this case — the local attached_local_plans row is keyed by lease_id, so retry-in-place is not available there either. Remedy: allow `(Probe, Probe, released=false)` with `role_index == 0` under the same predecessor-cleanup rule used for Primary, or document and test that a never-released probe always re-leases.","MEDIUM (safety, conditional on unsupplied migration guarantees) — The \"no Ticket means no OS release\" gate keys on the existence of a table row rather than on installed pairing state. Evidence: invocation.rs consume() reads `SELECT connected FROM attached_local_mode WHERE singleton=1` with `.optional()?` and then `if connected.is_none() && ticket.is_none() { return Ok(()) }` — i.e. a missing singleton row makes the ticketless native path legal. Everything else in this module treats pairing as installed state discovered elsewhere (request_attached_ticket calls check_authority_release() and re-runs initialize() because \"Pairing may have been explicitly installed after this Store opened\"; driver.rs calls installation::validate_store and installation::load). So a store that is paired on disk but whose attached_local_mode row is absent (partial migration, partial uninstall, restore from a pre-pairing snapshot) silently degrades to unauthorized starts rather than failing closed. Separately, consume() never re-checks ticket.configuration_sha256 against attached_local_mode.configuration_sha256; the only defense is the in-memory ReleaseBarrier's `state.configuration != ticket.configuration_sha256`, whose snapshot was read at challenge time and therefore cannot see a configuration change that lands between challenge and release. Remedy: derive the gate from installation::load(&self.paths.root) (or check_authority_release) rather than row presence, returning InvalidState when pairing is installed but the mode row is missing; and re-assert configuration_sha256 inside consume()'s existing `matches` query so the durable path does not depend solely on process memory.","LOW-MEDIUM (durability of the waiting record, coupling hazard) — The local waiting-outcome capture depends on the outbox being written in exactly two steps and on table creation order. Evidence: invocation.rs initialize() creates `attached_ticket_wait_outcome` only `AFTER UPDATE OF outcome_json ON attached_outbox`, and only when the `paired` probe (`SELECT EXISTS(... name='attached_outbox')`) succeeds at that moment. The included test proves the intended shape works (INSERT with NULL outcome, later UPDATE fires the trigger, subsequent `DELETE FROM attached_outbox` does not lose the record). But any accept() path that writes the outcome at INSERT time, or that replaces a row rather than updating it, produces no trigger firing and no attached_local_ticket_outcomes row; the retry loop in runtime.rs then never fires (retry_waiting_attached_ticket's join returns None) and the invocation silently degrades to the `until` deadline path, taking finding 2's orphan-ticket trace with it. SQLite does fire UPDATE triggers for `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`, so an upsert-style accept() is fine; a DELETE+INSERT or an insert-with-outcome is not. Remedy: either add the matching AFTER INSERT trigger with the same WHEN clause, or (preferable, since it removes the hidden coupling entirely) write the attached_local_ticket_outcomes row explicitly inside accept() in the same transaction, and assert in a test that a rejected reply always yields a local outcome row regardless of how the outbox row was materialized.","LOW (lock discipline, contradicts the rule stated in the same file) — driver.rs step() cancels barriers while holding the Store mutex. Evidence: `let mut store = lock(store)?;` shadows the parameter and the guard lives to the end of step(); after `tx.commit()?` the code calls `self.releases.accepted_rejection(&request, &reply.outcome)?`, which calls retire() -> barrier.cancel(). ReleaseState::disconnect()'s own doc says \"Never hold Store while canceling these barriers: release takes Store first, then its barrier, to order a concurrent cancellation commit.\" There is no deadlock (both paths acquire Store then barrier, and none of runtime.rs's release callbacks re-enter the barrier), but the driver will block on the barrier mutex for the full duration of a concurrent release — which includes the durable commit and `child.release()` ptrace work — while pinning the Store mutex that every runner thread needs. Given the 250 ms budget in finding 3, that self-inflicted stall is worth removing. Remedy: `drop(store);` immediately after tx.commit() and before accepted_rejection, matching the rule the file states.","LOW (evidence hygiene) — refresh_observation() persists a coordinator snapshot before deciding whether that coordinator's configuration is still the attached one. Evidence: driver.rs refresh_observation() calls `store.record_attached_machine_observation(&snapshot)?` and only afterwards runs `SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM attached_local_mode WHERE connected=1 AND configuration_sha256!=?1)` to raise \"coordinator configuration changed; full inventory is required\". So evidence captured under an unrecognized configuration is already durable when the session is fenced, and may subsequently feed Store::attached_observation_ready()/evaluate_admission on reconnect. The check is also skipped entirely while connected=0, which is exactly the window after a reconnect. This matches the comment's intent (\"Diagnostic evidence can fence a stale session, never authorize a new configuration\") only if record_attached_machine_observation stamps the snapshot with its configuration_sha256 and readers filter on it — not visible in the supplied files. Remedy: validate configuration_sha256 before recording, or store the hash alongside the observation and have admission reject observations whose configuration does not match the current attachment.","LOW (resource leak with a user-visible cliff) — Barrier registry entries are retired only on a durably accepted rejection or on a successful cleanup, so a cleanup failure leaks them until the next reconnect. Evidence: runtime.rs's cleanup closure calls `live.linux_releases.retire(job.invocation_id)?` only AFTER `live.linux.cleanup(...)?` and `record_attached_cleanup(...)?` both succeed — either `?` skips retire; ReleaseState::challenge enforces `if barriers.len() >= 1024 && !barriers.contains_key(&intent.invocation_id) { return Err(\"release registry capacity reached\") }`. Accumulated leaks therefore do not fail the leaking invocations, they fail unrelated NEW invocations with a confusing capacity error until a reconnect's disconnect() clears the map. Remedy: retire the barrier from a guard/Drop (or an unconditional tail block) so it is released regardless of cleanup outcome, since retiring the in-memory barrier is never itself cleanup proof.","LOW (retry precision) — retry_waiting_attached_ticket replays a stored intent against a refreshed grant without re-deriving the fields that depend on that grant. Evidence: invocation.rs retry_waiting_attached_ticket re-reads the grant (`SELECT grant_json FROM attached_grants WHERE allocation_key=?1 AND seal_json IS NULL`, requiring GrantState::Armed) and uses the CURRENT `grant.offer_nonce`, but enqueues `intent: serde_json::from_str(&intent)?` verbatim — release_sequence and previous_cleanup were computed in request_attached_ticket against the grant as it stood then. If grant.tickets advanced in between, machine_ticket.rs validate_next rejects with \"cleanup_incomplete\" (terminal per waiting_outcome), so the invocation fails hard instead of re-deriving a valid intent. This is fail-safe, not unsafe, and may be unreachable if one allocation can only ever have one live invocation at a time — worth stating that invariant explicitly rather than relying on it implicitly. Remedy: recompute release_sequence/previous_cleanup from the freshly read grant on retry (reusing the request_attached_ticket logic), or assert `grant.tickets.last()` is unchanged and fail with a distinguishable, retryable error if it is not."],"verdict":"findings"}

MEDIUM-HIGH (liveness/correctness, code-confirmed) — Transmission of AuthorizeInvocation is not gated on connected=1/reconciliation, so a reconnect during a ticket wait deterministically produces a Ticket the executor is forbidden to consume. Evidence: driver.rs connect() sets `UPDATE attached_local_mode SET connected=0` and only Outcome::Reconciled restores `connected=1`; step() transmits whatever manager::pending returns with no connected check; but invocation.rs consume() rejects with "Ticket belongs to a disconnected or different Invocation generation" whenever `connected != Some(true)`. Failure trace: invocation is waiting on op1; transport blips; new Driver::connect() sets connected=0 and begins recovery; step() finds op1 pending (recovery paging is only enqueued in the `manager::pending(...).is_none()` branch, so op1 is transmitted first, ahead of reconciliation); coordinator mints a Ticket; runtime.rs breaks its loop, retry_waiting_attached_ticket stops firing (its `NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM attached_tickets ...)` guard), barrier.release() runs commit -> mark_started_with_ticket/authorize_*_with_ticket -> consume() -> InvalidState because connected is still 0. The invocation fails, the ticket is left unconsumed, and case 2 above applies to its cleanup. Remedy: hold AuthorizeInvocation in the outbox until connected=1 (or explicitly prefer recovery/reconciliation commands over authorization commands in the pending selection), so the coordinator is never asked to mint a Ticket the executor cannot legally consume.

MEDIUM (correctness, hazard confirmed / classification unverifiable from supplied files) — Retryability of a rejection is decided by a hardcoded string list that is decoupled from the code that produces those strings, so a transient resource-contention rejection can be misclassified as fatal. Evidence: invocation.rs waiting_outcome() matches exactly `"quiet_waiting" | "quiet_contaminated" | "detector_unavailable" | "observation_stale" | "observation_missing" | "observation_unusable" | "observed_resource_busy" | "unavailable"`. machine_ticket.rs authorize() emits `Outcome::Rejected { code: blocker.code, detail: blocker.detail }` where `waiting = resource_blockers.first().or(context.non_quiet_blockers.first())` and `resource_blockers = physical.blockers(&readiness.config.resources, &active, &readiness.config.impact_incompatibilities)`. Only two producer codes are verifiable from the supplied text: "quiet_waiting" (in the list, correct) and "quiet_unattainable" (deliberately excluded and asserted terminal by the unit test). The codes minted by physical.blockers() for cpu_units/ram_mb/cargo_slots/gpu_slots/impacts, and by evaluate_request's non_quiet_blockers, are in files not supplied. If any of them is, say, "resource_busy" or "cargo_slots_exhausted" rather than "observed_resource_busy", then runtime.rs's `lock(store)?.attached_ticket(...)` turns a "wait for a free slot" answer into `StoreError::InvalidState("Invocation Ticket request did not grant release: ...")` and the invocation fails immediately instead of waiting out its budget — precisely the managed-Cargo contention path MR-3 exercises. Remedy: stop classifying on strings — carry retryability in the type (`Outcome::Rejected { code, detail, retryable: bool }` or a shared `enum BlockerCode`) so the coordinator that mints the blocker declares its transience; failing that, add a test that enumerates every Blocker code constructible by physical.blockers()/evaluate_request and asserts its waiting_outcome classification.

MEDIUM (correctness/liveness, code-confirmed in the supplied file) — A probe can never be re-authorized on its own Grant after a never-released or stale ticket. Evidence: machine_ticket.rs validate_next(): `AllocationOwner::Probe { invocation_id, .. } => previous.is_none() && intent.role == InvocationRole::Probe && ...`. For Work owners the file explicitly supports retry-in-place — `(InvocationRole::Primary, InvocationRole::Primary, false) => intent.role_index == 0` and `(Postcondition, Postcondition, false) => intent.role_index == last.role_index` — but the Probe arm has no analogue, so once one intent is in grant.tickets, any successor intent is rejected with code "conflict". Failure trace: probe invocation gets a Ticket; the release misses the 250 ms window (see the freshness finding) or yields Disposition::NeverReleased; cleanup is recorded with user_code_released=false; a retry on the same probe Lease/Grant is structurally impossible, so a single transient delay consumes the probe's whole allocation. This is safe (nothing is released twice) but converts a transient fault into an allocation-level failure. Confirm the runner obtains a fresh probe Lease/Grant in this case — the local attached_local_plans row is keyed by lease_id, so retry-in-place is not available there either. Remedy: allow `(Probe, Probe, released=false)` with `role_index == 0` under the same predecessor-cleanup rule used for Primary, or document and test that a never-released probe always re-leases.

MEDIUM (safety, conditional on unsupplied migration guarantees) — The "no Ticket means no OS release" gate keys on the existence of a table row rather than on installed pairing state. Evidence: invocation.rs consume() reads `SELECT connected FROM attached_local_mode WHERE singleton=1` with `.optional()?` and then `if connected.is_none() && ticket.is_none() { return Ok(()) }` — i.e. a missing singleton row makes the ticketless native path legal. Everything else in this module treats pairing as installed state discovered elsewhere (request_attached_ticket calls check_authority_release() and re-runs initialize() because "Pairing may have been explicitly installed after this Store opened"; driver.rs calls installation::validate_store and installation::load). So a store that is paired on disk but whose attached_local_mode row is absent (partial migration, partial uninstall, restore from a pre-pairing snapshot) silently degrades to unauthorized starts rather than failing closed. Separately, consume() never re-checks ticket.configuration_sha256 against attached_local_mode.configuration_sha256; the only defense is the in-memory ReleaseBarrier's `state.configuration != ticket.configuration_sha256`, whose snapshot was read at challenge time and therefore cannot see a configuration change that lands between challenge and release. Remedy: derive the gate from installation::load(&self.paths.root) (or check_authority_release) rather than row presence, returning InvalidState when pairing is installed but the mode row is missing; and re-assert configuration_sha256 inside consume()'s existing `matches` query so the durable path does not depend solely on process memory.

LOW-MEDIUM (durability of the waiting record, coupling hazard) — The local waiting-outcome capture depends on the outbox being written in exactly two steps and on table creation order. Evidence: invocation.rs initialize() creates `attached_ticket_wait_outcome` only `AFTER UPDATE OF outcome_json ON attached_outbox`, and only when the `paired` probe (`SELECT EXISTS(... name='attached_outbox')`) succeeds at that moment. The included test proves the intended shape works (INSERT with NULL outcome, later UPDATE fires the trigger, subsequent `DELETE FROM attached_outbox` does not lose the record). But any accept() path that writes the outcome at INSERT time, or that replaces a row rather than updating it, produces no trigger firing and no attached_local_ticket_outcomes row; the retry loop in runtime.rs then never fires (retry_waiting_attached_ticket's join returns None) and the invocation silently degrades to the `until` deadline path, taking finding 2's orphan-ticket trace with it. SQLite does fire UPDATE triggers for `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`, so an upsert-style accept() is fine; a DELETE+INSERT or an insert-with-outcome is not. Remedy: either add the matching AFTER INSERT trigger with the same WHEN clause, or (preferable, since it removes the hidden coupling entirely) write the attached_local_ticket_outcomes row explicitly inside accept() in the same transaction, and assert in a test that a rejected reply always yields a local outcome row regardless of how the outbox row was materialized.

LOW (lock discipline, contradicts the rule stated in the same file) — driver.rs step() cancels barriers while holding the Store mutex. Evidence: `let mut store = lock(store)?;` shadows the parameter and the guard lives to the end of step(); after `tx.commit()?` the code calls `self.releases.accepted_rejection(&request, &reply.outcome)?`, which calls retire() -> barrier.cancel(). ReleaseState::disconnect()'s own doc says "Never hold Store while canceling these barriers: release takes Store first, then its barrier, to order a concurrent cancellation commit." There is no deadlock (both paths acquire Store then barrier, and none of runtime.rs's release callbacks re-enter the barrier), but the driver will block on the barrier mutex for the full duration of a concurrent release — which includes the durable commit and `child.release()` ptrace work — while pinning the Store mutex that every runner thread needs. Given the 250 ms budget in finding 3, that self-inflicted stall is worth removing. Remedy: `drop(store);` immediately after tx.commit() and before accepted_rejection, matching the rule the file states.

LOW (evidence hygiene) — refresh_observation() persists a coordinator snapshot before deciding whether that coordinator's configuration is still the attached one. Evidence: driver.rs refresh_observation() calls `store.record_attached_machine_observation(&snapshot)?` and only afterwards runs `SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM attached_local_mode WHERE connected=1 AND configuration_sha256!=?1)` to raise "coordinator configuration changed; full inventory is required". So evidence captured under an unrecognized configuration is already durable when the session is fenced, and may subsequently feed Store::attached_observation_ready()/evaluate_admission on reconnect. The check is also skipped entirely while connected=0, which is exactly the window after a reconnect. This matches the comment's intent ("Diagnostic evidence can fence a stale session, never authorize a new configuration") only if record_attached_machine_observation stamps the snapshot with its configuration_sha256 and readers filter on it — not visible in the supplied files. Remedy: validate configuration_sha256 before recording, or store the hash alongside the observation and have admission reject observations whose configuration does not match the current attachment.

LOW (resource leak with a user-visible cliff) — Barrier registry entries are retired only on a durably accepted rejection or on a successful cleanup, so a cleanup failure leaks them until the next reconnect. Evidence: runtime.rs's cleanup closure calls `live.linux_releases.retire(job.invocation_id)?` only AFTER `live.linux.cleanup(...)?` and `record_attached_cleanup(...)?` both succeed — either `?` skips retire; ReleaseState::challenge enforces `if barriers.len() >= 1024 && !barriers.contains_key(&intent.invocation_id) { return Err("release registry capacity reached") }`. Accumulated leaks therefore do not fail the leaking invocations, they fail unrelated NEW invocations with a confusing capacity error until a reconnect's disconnect() clears the map. Remedy: retire the barrier from a guard/Drop (or an unconditional tail block) so it is released regardless of cleanup outcome, since retiring the in-memory barrier is never itself cleanup proof.

LOW (retry precision) — retry_waiting_attached_ticket replays a stored intent against a refreshed grant without re-deriving the fields that depend on that grant. Evidence: invocation.rs retry_waiting_attached_ticket re-reads the grant (`SELECT grant_json FROM attached_grants WHERE allocation_key=?1 AND seal_json IS NULL`, requiring GrantState::Armed) and uses the CURRENT `grant.offer_nonce`, but enqueues `intent: serde_json::from_str(&intent)?` verbatim — release_sequence and previous_cleanup were computed in request_attached_ticket against the grant as it stood then. If grant.tickets advanced in between, machine_ticket.rs validate_next rejects with "cleanup_incomplete" (terminal per waiting_outcome), so the invocation fails hard instead of re-deriving a valid intent. This is fail-safe, not unsafe, and may be unreachable if one allocation can only ever have one live invocation at a time — worth stating that invariant explicitly rather than relying on it implicitly. Remedy: recompute release_sequence/previous_cleanup from the freshly read grant on retry (reusing the request_attached_ticket logic), or assert `grant.tickets.last()` is unchanged and fail with a distinguishable, retryable error if it is not.
